Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for Australia Women's response with the bat. Harmanpreet Kaur has her troops in a huddle before they take their places on the field. Alyssa Healy walks out to open the innings alongside Phoebe Litchfield. Amanjot Kaur will kickstart the proceedings for India. Kaur to Healy with a slip in place. Let's play...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Right then, Australia will be fairly pleased to have limited the damage. The highest successful chase in Women’s ODIs stands at 302, but if any team can pull it off, it’s this Australian side, which bats deep, all the way down to number 10, with Alana King fresh off a half-century. The pitch has played true for the most part, apart from some gentle turn for the spinners. However, with dew expected to arrive, batting could get even easier in the second innings. The Indian pacers will need to take a cue from the way Annabel Sutherland bowled into the surface and took the pace off to be effective. It is all set up for an intriguing chase.

Pratika Rawal is up for a chat. She expresses her delight about the partnership with Smriti Mandhana, stating she's a big fan of Mandhana's game. Shares that she is thrilled about the century stand and acknowledges the challenging period with dot balls in between, but was satisfied with converting them into runs later. Adds that she played to her strengths, noting that she only took shots on her back foot when she was confident of hitting boundaries or sixes.

A timely double strike from Australia, however, meant that India were once again forced into rebuilding, and they found a brisk partnership through Richa Ghosh and Jemimah Rodrigues. At 287/4 with 8 overs to go and Ghosh and Jemimah set at the crease, the team in blue looked on course for a lot more, especially with Megan Schutt walking off the field after pulling up. Sutherland broke that flourishing stand, and from there, the Aussies kept chipping away at the wickets courtesy of Sutherland and the spinners. India lost their last 6 wickets for just 36 runs, with Annabel Sutherland finishing with a superb five-wicket haul.

Australia found it difficult to stem the flow of runs, and although Rawal seemed to be getting bogged down at one stage, Mandhana’s ability to pick up boundaries took the pressure off her during the 155-run opening stand. Smriti broke a couple of records along the way in her 80-run knock, becoming the first batter to score 1,000 runs in Women’s ODI cricket in a calendar year and also the fastest to reach 5,000 runs in ODIs in just 112 innings. After Mandhana’s departure, India’s innings had been hitting a wall, with runs drying up completely in previous games, but Harleen Deol and Harmanpreet Kaur kept the momentum going.

A fine effort from Australia to pull things back! At 192/1 at the end of 30 overs, India looked set to run away, but they were superbly halted in their tracks by the Aussies. It is not often that you can say a batting side has left a few runs out there after posting 330, but that is exactly the case tonight. After being asked to bat first, Smriti Mandhana and Pratika Rawal were watchful in their approach, but with the introduction of Sophie Molineux inside the Powerplay and her opening over going for 16 runs, India were well on their way.

India's head coach, Amol Muzumdar, is up for a chat. He says that the top-order haven't yet performed in the campaign, which is the scariest part for their opponents, but he continues to believe in them as they hold the capability to do wonders. Also says that he is happy with his middle order, who are anchoring the inning and wishes they continue their good work throughout the campaign.

The Indian captain, Harmanpreet Kaur believes that this looks like a better wicket than the last game and hopes that they can put up a decent total on the board. Informs that they are unchanged for this game. Reckons that it is important how you bounce back from a loss and shares that after the defeat, they all sat together and talked about the positives. Adds that the last 5 overs did not go their way against South Africa, but they were in the game for 95 overs, which is one of the positives. Mentions that the crowd support has always been important and is one of the biggest parts of their lives.

Alyssa Healy, the skipper of Australia, says that they would like to bowl first, as last night when they were training, it got a bit dewy. She also states that they have one change in the line up as Sophie Molineux comes in for Georgia Wareham. Mentions that this is her first time in Vizag since 2011. Ends up saying that the atmosphere is massive and the girls are pumped up.

Australia Women (Playing XI) - Alyssa Healy (C/WK), Phoebe Litchfield, Ellyse Perry, Beth Mooney, Annabel Sutherland, Ashleigh Gardner, Tahlia McGrath, Sophie Molineux (In for Georgia Wareham), Kim Garth, Alana King, Megan Schutt.

India Women (Unchanged Playing XI) - Pratika Rawal, Smriti Mandhana, Harleen Deol, Harmanpreet Kaur (C), Jemimah Rodrigues, Deepti Sharma, Amanjot Kaur, Richa Ghosh (WK), Sneh Rana, Kranti Gaud, Sree Charani.
TOSS - Alyssa Healy calls it correctly and Australia will BOWL first.

PITCH REPORT - Former Indian skipper, Mithali Raj gives us a lowdown on the conditions. Mentions that the surface looks hard and it has been rolled nicely. Believes that this will not be a one-way traffic, as if the bowlers hit the right areas and keep the stumps in play, they will definitely be in the game.

Australia, on the other hand, start this match with momentum behind them. Although they stumbled early, they bounced back emphatically in their win over Pakistan, where Beth Mooney played a match-defining century after her side was reeling at 76/7. The defending champions also boast firepower in Ashleigh Gardner, whose century against New Zealand set the tournament alight. On the bowling side, the likes of Kim Garth and Megan Schutt will have a big role to play against the misfiring Indian top-order.  Will India make their comeback after the previous loss, or will Australia secure the two crucial points to climb to the top of the table? So many questions buzzing around, but to find out the answer, stay tuned with us as the toss and team updates are coming up.

India have had a mixed campaign so far. While they managed to secure wins over Sri Lanka and Pakistan, albeit in scratchy fashion, they were left stunned by South Africa a few nights ago here in Visakhapatnam. Their top order has not quite clicked into gear yet, and it was the young wicketkeeper-batter Richa Ghosh who produced a rescue act under pressure against South Africa. On the bowling front, Deepti Sharma leads India’s attack with 7 wickets so far, and will be expected to deliver through her control and variation. Skipper, Harmanpreet Kaur, will want to take more responsibility herself to challenge the might of the Aussie bowling unit.

We are approaching the halfway mark of the round robin stage at the 2025 Women’s World Cup, and match 13 promises to be a blockbuster as India take on Australia at the Dr. Y. S. Rajasekhara Reddy ACA-VDCA Cricket Stadium in Visakhapatnam. Ever since the fixtures were announced, this clash has stood out as one of the marquee encounters of the tournament, and the buzz surrounding it is evident with tickets for the game already sold out. Starting with the hosts, India began their campaign with wins over Asian rivals Sri Lanka and Pakistan. They were not at their absolute best in either game, but managed to find ways to get the job done. However, the schedule has now entered a crucial phase with four high-profile fixtures against South Africa, Australia, England and New Zealand. That run has not begun well, as Nadine de Klerk’s brilliance powered South Africa to a stunning victory that left Harmanpreet Kaur’s side reeling. The loss would have hurt, but with only a short turnaround between games, India have little time to dwell and plenty of motivation to bounce back against the defending champions. In two of their three games, it has been the lower order that has come to their rescue. Richa Ghosh’s valiant 94 against South Africa dug the team out of a hole and took them to 251, but it did not prove enough on the night. The Indian think tank may need to reassess their balance, as while the side bats deep till number nine, it leaves them with only five specialist bowling options, which makes them look slightly short with the ball. Bringing in a sixth bowling option, in Renuka Singh Thakur or even Radha Yadav, would strengthen the attack, but it would require dropping a batter. The experienced names like Smriti Mandhana, Jemimah Rodrigues and captain Harmanpreet Kaur have not had much of an impact so far, and if India are to challenge a strong Australian side, they need these players to fire. Another talking point has been the slowdown in scoring after the Powerplay, often caused by Mandhana’s early dismissal and the likes of Pratika Rawal and Harleen Deol getting bogged down against spin. They will need to improve in terms of strike rotation. Turning to Australia, the defending champions have two wins from three matches, with the other being a washout against Sri Lanka. Their previous win against Pakistan showcased their trademark resilience, as they recovered from 76/7 to register a 107-run victory. Beth Mooney’s century bailed them out of deep trouble, while Alana King’s maiden ODI half-century at number ten spoke volumes about Australia’s batting depth. Ashleigh Gardner and Mooney already have centuries to their names, but apart from them, Alyssa Healy, Phoebe Litchfield, Ellyse Perry, Annabel Sutherland and Tahlia McGrath have not quite set the tournament alight and will be eager to change that. The Australians have endured collapses in both of their completed games, finding themselves in trouble after promising starts, something they will look to avoid against India. Considering India’s struggles against left-arm spin, having lost 12 wickets in three matches, Healy and the Australian management may be tempted to recall Sophie Molineux after her impressive three-wicket haul against New Zealand. Alternatively, they could continue with their two leg spinners, Alana King and Georgia Wareham, whose stock deliveries turn away from the right-handers, seven of whom feature in India’s top nine and can contribute with the bat. Kim Garth and Megan Schutt were impressive with the new ball against Pakistan, and their impact with the new ball will be crucial once again. India’s batting has relied heavily on brisk starts provided by Mandhana, and if she falls early, the top order could find itself under pressure. Australia will be keen to exploit that vulnerability and seize the early momentum. Just before the World Cup, these two sides faced off in an ODI series that Australia won 2-1. The series decider in Delhi was an absolute run fest, producing a match aggregate of 781 runs, the highest in Women’s ODI cricket. However, if the contest between India and South Africa in Visakhapatnam was anything to go by, run scoring may not be as easy, and the conditions could favour the spinners. It could ultimately come down to which team handles spin better. Since Harmanpreet Kaur’s sensational unbeaten 171 in the 2017 World Cup semifinal, the team in blue has managed to win only 2 of their 16 ODI meetings against Australia. Can Kaur and her team rise to the challenge and come out on top against the defending champions, or will Healy’s side extend their dominance with another win? We shall find out.
